title: Video deepfakes in business email compromise
body_md:
## A meeting is another channel, not a payment authorisation

Business email compromise (BEC) aims to redirect a transfer or change the account behind a real invoice. An attacker may control a lookalike address, a compromised mailbox, a chat account or a meeting invitation. A video can add social proof, but the decision still concerns *who authorised this exact payment to this exact beneficiary*.

In a January 2024 case described by the Hong Kong Government in June that year, a worker received a phishing email purporting to be a UK CFO. The worker saw a **pre-recorded fabricated group conference**, authorised transfers to five local accounts, and received further instructions by instant message. The reported loss was about HK$200 million; the case was still under investigation at the time of the official reply. This is a documented example of a recorded presentation, not evidence that the impostors held a live interactive discussion. Our exercises below are fictional.

An attacker can choose the meeting platform and arrange familiar faces and voices. Another legitimate explanation for odd video is compression, a virtual background or poor lighting. Asking someone to turn their head may raise a concern but cannot authorise a wire: a convincing recording may not show artifacts, and a real colleague may freeze on screen. Treat a call as information about a request, not as the control that releases money.

For a payment or beneficiary change, compare the new instructions with the existing vendor record. Use a known number from records created before the request, obtain the required separate approval, and record what was verified. A message from a genuine internal account is not always enough if that account is compromised. If a manager cannot be reached, hold the change and escalate by the documented route. Confidentiality is never a reason to bypass that route. If a transfer has already gone out, contact the bank immediately to ask about recall; recovery is uncertain.

**Practical boundary:** use the same control for a normal call, a video call and a polished email. The technology of the impersonation can change; the beneficiary verification and authority chain should not.

widget_config.goal: Apply payment-change controls even when a request is presented in a convincing video meeting.
widget_config.today_action: Find your organisation’s existing rule for approving a new beneficiary and identify the independent callback contact.
widget_config.scope: Workplace education; the Hong Kong example is a dated 2024 official account and US IC3 advice is jurisdiction-specific. Follow your own employer and bank procedures.

sources.title: Hong Kong Government: Legislative Council reply on deepfake fraud
sources.scope: Dated 26 June 2024; reports a January case with a prerecorded fabricated conference and later messaging instructions. Investigation was ongoing at that date; not a live interactive-call example.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance for transfer and account-change requests; secondary-channel verification and urgent bank contact after a suspected transfer. Organisational and national procedures vary.

blocks.title: The “CFO” confirms a new account on video
blocks.situation: A synthetic meeting shows the CFO and two colleagues; a chat message says a supplier’s bank account changed this morning and a transfer must happen now.
blocks.analysis: Multiple faces and the chat are not independent approval. Hold the change, call the supplier and CFO using pre-existing records, and complete the separate sign-off. The video could be generated, recorded or genuine with a compromised account; the control is the same.

blocks.title: A legitimate call has strange lighting
blocks.situation: Synthetic example: A known vendor on a routine video call freezes and appears out of sync. The existing invoice and destination account are unchanged.
blocks.analysis: Compression can cause these effects. Do not call the vendor a fraudster from pixels alone. Reconnect through the established meeting route if the conversation matters, and continue normal invoice checks.

blocks.title: The acquisition meeting
blocks.setup: Synthetic scenario: a fictional finance team receives an invitation to an urgent video meeting about a changed escrow recipient. Each decision is a separate snapshot; actions in one do not carry into the next.

steps.prompt: A familiar face says the deal is confidential. What do you record?

choices.explanation: Faces do not describe the account change.

choices.text: The exact new recipient and requested action
choices.consequence: You define the change requiring verification.
choices.explanation: A general “CFO approved” is too vague to validate the beneficiary.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: the invitation includes a supplier callback number. Which number do you use?

choices.text: Call the supplier through the number already in vendor records
choices.consequence: The call leaves the invitation’s controlled context.
choices.explanation: A number introduced with the change may belong to the attacker.

choices.text: Call the number in the invitation
choices.consequence: A cooperating voice confirms the same false instruction.
choices.explanation: This is a second call, but not an independent source.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you call the supplier using the number already in vendor records, but get no answer. The meeting demands approval now. What do you do?

choices.text: Hold the beneficiary change and use the escalation/sign-off route
choices.consequence: The deadline passes without an unverified transfer.
choices.explanation: No response is not consent; confidentiality does not suspend controls.

choices.text: Approve because the group call counts as two witnesses
choices.consequence: In this simulation the funds go to the wrong recipient.
choices.explanation: Participants inside one meeting may share the same compromised source.

blocks.debrief: The Hong Kong case shows why video cannot itself serve as the payment control. This fictional exercise adds independent vendor verification and a separate approval. Retry any step to compare consequences.

questions.prompt: Does a live-looking group call prove a payment change is authorised?

choices.text: No; verify beneficiary and authority through separate records
choices.explanation: Media appearance and payment authority are different questions.
Several images can be supplied through one controlled call.

questions.prompt: The vendor’s camera glitches during a routine unchanged invoice. What follows?

choices.explanation: Compression artifacts are not a reliable verdict.

choices.text: Continue normal checks and reconnect if needed
choices.explanation: A glitch can be benign and does not settle identity or fraud.

questions.prompt: A transfer was made to a suspected impostor account. First practical response?

choices.text: Wait for the meeting organiser to explain
choices.explanation: Delay can reduce the chance of any recovery.

choices.text: Contact the sending bank promptly about recall
choices.explanation: Timing matters, though recovery is not guaranteed.
